title: Labor powerbrokers cut AI deal for workers
description: Labor will respond to growing anxiety about the rise of artificial intelligence with a new taskforce to give Australian workers a greater say in how the technology shapes the nation.

author: Clare Armstrong
full_text: Labor to back Fair AI Taskforce to give workers a say over artificial intelligence Wed 22 Jul 2026 at 10:23pm , updatedThu 23 Jul 2026 at 7:49am In short: Labor members will back a national artificial intelligence taskforce bringing together workers, unions and experts to help shape the debate over AI. The proposal would promote AI education and digital skills while giving the labour movement a bigger role in discussions about the technology’s impact. What's next? Delegates will vote on the amendment at Labor's national conference where the party's platform will be finalised this week. Labor will respond to growing anxiety about the rise of artificial intelligence with a new taskforce to give Australian workers a greater say in how the technology shapes the nation. Delegates are expected to endorse an amendment to the ALP's draft platform establishing a Fair AI Taskforce after a deal was brokered ahead of the party's 50th National Conference in Adelaide on Thursday. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will use a keynote address at the opening of the three-day conference to announce the expansion of Labor's paid prac scheme to students in ten additional healthcare professions. The ABC can reveal an agreement was reached late on Wednesday on an amendment pushed by Labor's Right faction to ensure workers and unions are able to help shape how AI impacts Australian workplaces. AI job losses and workforce disruption have been a key concern in behind-the-scenes talks, with the breakthrough potentially reducing the chance of a policy brawl on the conference floor. But negotiations remain ongoing on a range of other issues, including funding for local governments, the taxation of natural resources and gambling reform. Labor to establish AI taskforce The proposed national Fair AI Taskforce would bring together unions, rank-and-file Labor members and artificial intelligence experts to develop AI policy ideas. The new body would operate through the Chifley Research Centre and advocate for wider access to AI education and digital skills training. It would also "build awareness among members, unions, and the broader community of the opportunities and risks AI presents". Senior Right figure and NSW Senator Tony Sheldon said there was "no denying" the value AI could create, but the value must flow through to and benefit all Australians rather than be "concentrated" in the hands of global tech giants. "We cannot outsource Australia's future to tech bros," he said. Senator Sheldon argued AI was a "tool" for work, not a decision maker, insisting things like judgement, context, nuance, common sense or empathy could not be programmed into an algorithm. "Human intelligence should be the final arbiter of every decision," he said. The move comes a week after Mr Albanese unveiled plans for a national AI framework, an Office of AI and mandatory standards for data centres, arguing Australia should help shape the AI revolution rather than simply respond to it. One Labor source said Mr Albanese's address had calmed AI anxiety within the party ahead of conference but expected in the "longer term" the government's response to the technology would remain a "contentious" issue internally. PM says One Nation ‘rage’ doesn’t take country forward In his speech on the first day of the triennial conference, Mr Albanese will acknowledge cost of living pressures and the feeling many people have that the economy is "simply not working for them". “That goes deeper than sentiment, it’s a reality people are up against,” he will say. Mr Albanese will argue his government’s focus on “practical measures that matter to people and make a positive difference on their lives” is how Labor can prove “the status quo is not set in stone”. “That is how we demonstrate to Australians that their hard work will pay off, that their effort is worth it, that they can plan and build for their future,” he will say. In a thinly veiled rebuke of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, Mr Albanese will also criticise politicians who play up grievances and unfairly blame problems on others. “A list of problems only counts for something if it comes with solutions,” he will say. “And while you can go a long way in politics, for a long time, by raging against a system that you are a part of, without a plan to fix it. "Or blaming people who cannot defend themselves for a problem they did not cause. “That doesn’t build anything. It doesn’t change anything. It doesn’t take our country forward.” Paid prac expanded to more healthcare students Mr Albanese will also announce the expansion of the Commonwealth Prac Payment scheme to include students of clinical psychology, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech pathology, para medicine, radiography, pharmacy, rehabilitation therapies, audiology and podiatry. Since last year, Australians studying teaching, nursing, midwifery and social work have been able to access payment while undertaking placements for their studies. Students studying medicine or veterinary courses have not been granted access to the paid prac scheme. Eligible students currently receive $338.60 per week during their clinical and professional placement periods, with the payment means tested and indexed annually. Mr Albanese said expanding paid prac would help more Australians get the qualifications the nation needed. “This is an investment in our future healthcare workforce,” he said. Health Minister Mark Butler said students from the bush who faced an “extra cost” training away from home would particularly benefit. “This expansion means that if you’re training to be a pharmacist, physio or psychologist, you’ll also now have a bit of extra help to get through,” he said. Education Minister Jason Clare said paid prac was already making a difference for students training in a range of areas, which was why the government was expanding it. “This will help more students finish their qualifications and move into the jobs the country needs,” he said. Gambling, gas and super talks ahead of conference Policy fights on gambling harm reduction, a gas export tax and local government funding are brewing ahead of the conference, though not every issue is expected to result in a debate among delegates on the floor. Party powerbrokers and unions are also in talks on issues such as improving dental access through Medicare, compulsory superannuation for under-18s and the creation of an independent aviation body. Multiple Labor sources have told the ABC efforts are underway to progress amendments to Labor's draft national platform on gambling after the suite of changes unveiled by Mr Albanese earlier this year did not include the establishment of a national watchdog. During the conference former treasurer and outgoing ALP President Wayne Swan as well as former indigenous affairs minister Linda Burney will both be awarded National Life Membership of the party. Mr Albanese said Mr Swann had “dedicated his life to improving the lot of working Australians,” while Ms Burney was a “trail blazer” as the first Indigenous woman elected to the House of Representatives.
